newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African police consider new probe in Malan case.
newsitem.headline: S.African police consider new probe in Malan case.

text.p: South African police are considering resuming the hunt for the killers of 13 blacks after former defence chief Magnus Malan was acquitted of masterminding the murders, the country's top policeman said on Monday.
Malan and other top officers were acquitted of the 1987 killings last week.
Police Commissioner George Fivaz said in a statement the real killers still roamed free.
"It...cannot be automatically assumed that the KwaMakhutha massacre must now be regarded as closed and that the real killers must go undetected," he said.
"The acquittal of General Magnus Malan and others...requires examining the feasibility of reopening investigations into the killings."

Fivaz said police would study Judge Jan Hugo's ruling, which slammed the prosecution case and dubbed key state witnesses liars and unreliable. They would also look at Hugo's criticism of the detective work.

Malan, the most senior apartheid official to be tried for atrocities in the defence of white rule, was cleared of masterminding the attack on the home of a supporter of Nelson Mandela's then-banned African National Congress (ANC).
The state argued that the massacre near the Indian Ocean port of Durban was part of a military operation of support for the ANC's mainly Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) rivals.

Sydney Mufamadi, Mandela's minister of police, said his ministry took Hugo's criticism of the investigation seriously, and wanted to ensure that future investigations met "the highest possible standards".

The unit responsible for the case against Malan and his 19 co-accused was set up by Mufamadi to probe death-squads operating in the last decade of white rule under then-president F.W. de Klerk's National Party government.
Mandela's ANC slammed de Klerk on Monday, accusing him of showing no sorrow for those who were massacred -- among them women and children.
De Klerk, the country's last white ruler, said after Malan and the others were acquitted that the eight-month trial was misguided and should not have taken place.
"Mr de Klerk has demonstrated that he is only interested in protecting himself and the (National Party) power clique that abused our country...
"Mr de Klerk has been celebrating with such indecent joy that not a single word of sympathy for the victims of the massacre or their family members has been uttered," an ANC statement said.

The ANC accused de Klerk's party, which left Mandela's government of national unity for the opposition benches in June this year, of being the "main instigator and perpetrator of violence" in the Zulu heartland province.
